title: The number that jailed a mother

beats.narration: One multiplication put a mother in prison for life.

Sally Clark, a solicitor, lost both of her infant sons in cot deaths, thirteen months apart. At her trial a paediatrician told the jury the odds of that happening naturally were one in seventy-three million. He got that number by squaring.

Two probabilities multiply cleanly only when one event has no effect on the other. A family that has already lost a baby to sudden infant death is not a random family, and the Royal Statistical Society said so in writing. The correct joint uses a conditional. When the chance of a second death, given the first, is bigger than the base rate, the true joint is bigger too, and the seventy-three million evaporates.
Her conviction was overturned in 2003. She died four years later. The Royal Statistical Society still cites her trial when it warns courts about the misuse of statistics.
beats.display: Independence is a claim. Not a default.

mechanism: Two probabilities multiply as P(A)·P(B) only when the events are independent — when knowing A happened tells you nothing about B. Meadow squared a single-SIDS base rate as though the two deaths were drawn from unrelated families, producing about one in seventy-three million. The general identity is P(A ∩ B) = P(A)·P(B | A); it only collapses to the product when P(B | A) equals P(B). The Royal Statistical Society argued that within one family — for genetic and environmental reasons — P(B | A) is much larger than P(B), so the true joint is orders of magnitude larger than Meadow's number.

facts.claim: Sally Clark was convicted by a 10–2 majority verdict on 9 November 1999.
facts.quote: Clark was convicted by a 10–2 majority verdict on 9 November 1999,

facts.claim: The prosecution paediatrician reached his figure by squaring a single-SIDS base rate.
facts.quote: He had arrived at this figure by squaring his estimate of a chance of 1 in 8500 of an individual SIDS death in similar circumstances.

facts.claim: The figure quoted at trial was 1 in 73 million, computed as 8543 × 8543.
facts.quote: the probability of two in the same family was around "1 in 73 million" (8543 × 8543).

facts.claim: In October 2001 the Royal Statistical Society publicly criticised the misuse of statistics in her trial.
facts.quote: In October 2001, the Royal Statistical Society (RSS) issued a public statement expressing its concern at the "misuse of statistics in the courts".

facts.claim: Her convictions were overturned in January 2003, on her second appeal.
facts.quote: her convictions were overturned at her second appeal in January 2003.

facts.claim: Sally Clark was found dead in her home on 16 March 2007.
facts.quote: Clark was found dead in her home in Hatfield Peverel in Essex on 16 March 2007.

facts.claim: Her second son, Harry, was found dead on 26 January 1998, aged 8 weeks.
facts.quote: However, he was also found dead on 26 January 1998, aged 8 weeks.

facts.claim: Squaring a single-SIDS likelihood does not soundly estimate the likelihood of two SIDS deaths in the same family.
facts.quote: The likelihood of two SIDS deaths in the same family cannot be soundly estimated by squaring the likelihood of a single such death in all otherwise similar families.
